variables.content: The electronic confinement produced by the anti-lattice of carbon monoxide (CO) molecules on Cu(111) is modeled by a single-orbital tight-binding Hamiltonian with uniform on-site energy ε, nearest-neighbor hopping t_nn, next-nearest-neighbor hopping t_nnn, and nearest-neighbor overlap s. Nonlinear least-squares fitting to muffin-tin band-structure calculations yields the parameter values ε = 0.107 eV, t_nn = −0.121 eV, t_nnn = −0.028 eV, and s = 0.293. These parameters are used in tight-binding calculations that reproduce the measured local density of states (LDOS) and differential conductance maps.
variables.title: Tight-binding parametrization of the artificial-lattice Hamiltonian fitted to muffin-tin calculations

variables.content:
For the one-dimensional tight-binding Hamiltonian
$$
H=\sum_{n=1}^{N-1} c_{n}|n\rangle\langle n+1|+c_{n}^{*}|n+1\rangle\langle n|,
$$
consider the perturbed Hamiltonian $H'=H+f|1\rangle\langle1|$ with scalar $f\in\mathbb{R}$, and denote the eigenvalues of $H$ as $\{e_k\}$ and those of $H'$ as $\{e'_k\}$. Then the local eigenstate weights $|\langle1|e_k\rangle|^2$ are given by
$$
|\langle e_k|1\rangle|^{2}=\frac{(e_{k}^{\prime}-e_{k})}{f}\prod_{m\neq k}\frac{(e_{k}-e_{m}^{\prime})}{(e_{k}-e_{m})}.
$$
Knowledge of $\{e_k\}$ and $\{|\langle1|e_k\rangle|^2\}$ determines all hopping parameters $\{c_n\}$. Concretely, the moment equations
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{N} e_{k}^{m} |\langle1|e_{k}\rangle|^{2}=\langle1|H^{m}|1\rangle
$$
for integers $m$ generate a system of polynomial relations in the $c_n$ which can be solved iteratively: for example $m=2$ yields $c_{1}^{2}$, $m=4$ yields combinations involving $c_{1}^{2}+c_{2}^{2}$, and higher $m$ successively reveal the remaining $c_n$. On-site potential terms $b_{n}|n\rangle\langle n|$ can similarly be recovered from the same data.
variables.title: Reconstruction of tight-binding couplings from spectra and local eigenstate weights

variables.content: The reduced tight-binding Hamiltonian is written as $H=\varepsilon_i \delta_{ij}+t_{ij}[a_i^\dagger b_j]$, where $\varepsilon_i$ is the on-site energy, $t_{ij}$ is the hopping integral between orbitals $i$ and $j$, and the parameters are fitted from local-density-approximation calculations.
variables.title: The tight-binding Hamiltonian is parameterized by on-site energies and hopping integrals fitted from LDA calculations

otin\{\ell,k\}} t( oldsymbol{u}_{\ell m}, oldsymbol{u}_{k m})+\delta_{\ell k} v_\ell \mathrm{Id}_{N_{\mathrm{b}}}$, where $ oldsymbol{u}_{\ell k}=( oldsymbol{r}_k- oldsymbol{r}_\ell, v_\ell, v_k, Z_\ell, Z_k)$ and $N_{\mathrm{b}}$ is the number of atomic orbitals per atom, with $h$ and $t$ matrix-valued functions satisfying exponential decay bounds $|h( oldsymbol{u}_{\ell k})|+|
abla h( oldsymbol{u}_{\ell k})|\le h_0 e^{-\gamma_0 r_{\ell k}}$ and $|t( oldsymbol{u}_{\ell m}, oldsymbol{u}_{k m})|+|
abla t( oldsymbol{u}_{\ell m}, oldsymbol{u}_{k m})|\le h_0 e^{-\gamma_0(r_{\ell m}+r_{k m})}$ for constants $h_0,\gamma_0>0$ where $r_{\ell m}=| oldsymbol{r}_\ell- oldsymbol{r}_m|$, and given any finite set of interpolation nodes $X=\{x_j\}$, the interpolated atomic observable $I_X O_\ell( oldsymbol{u}) := \mathrm{tr} ig[I_X O(\mathcal{H}( oldsymbol{u}))_{\ell\ell} ig]$ is representable exactly as a finite body-order site energy of the form $I_X O_\ell( oldsymbol{u})=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\sum_{k_1<\cdots<k_n
eq\ell} V_{nN}( oldsymbol{u}_\ell; oldsymbol{u}_{\ell k_1},\dots, oldsymbol{u}_{\ell k_n})$ with $N=|X|$ and with maximal body-order at most $2(|X|-1)$ for the three-centre model, or $|X|-1$ in the two-centre simplification where $t\equiv0$. Each $V_{nN}$ depends only on the finite set $\{ oldsymbol{u}_\ell, oldsymbol{u}_{\ell k_j}\}$ and is constructed by collecting terms from the monomial expansion of $I_X O(\mathcal{H})$.
variables.title: Polynomial interpolation yields finite body-order site energies

variables.content: The Structure Preserving Transformation (SPT) framework yields an indicator condition for the existence of “economic” Hamiltonian identification algorithms whose computational complexity scales with the number of unknown parameters $\mathcal{M}$ rather than the full system dimension $d$. Specifically, if one can realize elementary probe/measurement pairs such that $B=I_{\sigma j}$ and $C=I_{i\sigma}$ (i.e., the initial state equals the $j$th canonical basis vector and the measured observable selects the $i$th state component), which isolates the unknown Hamiltonian parameter appearing as $A_{ij}$, then identification of one unknown parameter under that setting is possible and the total Hamiltonian can be obtained by repeating this procedure parameterwise; this structural indicator is computable via SPT/Similarity Transformation Approach (STA) analysis on the minimal subsystem and signals when algorithmic cost can be made $O(\mathcal{M} \cdot f(\mathcal{M}))$ for some function $f$ independent of $d$.

related.content:
For the $(n+1)\times(n+1)$ antisymmetric tridiagonal system matrix
      $$
      A=\begin{pmatrix}
      0 & \theta_1 & 0 & \cdots \\
      -\theta_1 & 0 & \theta_2 & \\
      0 & -\theta_2 & 0 & \ddots \\
      \vdots & & \ddots & \ddots
      \end{pmatrix},
      $$
      with probe initial vector $B=\mathbf{x}_0=(1,0,\dots,0)^T$ and output selector $C=(1,0,\dots,0)$ (this model arises from the exchange spin chain without transverse field, with Hamiltonian $H=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{(-1)^{i+1} \theta_{i}}{2}\left(X_{i} X_{i+1}+Y_{i} Y_{i+1}\right)$), the realization is almost always controllable and observable (hence minimal), and the STA equations constrained by $S\mathbf{x}_0=\mathbf{x}_0$, $C=CS$ admit only solutions for which $S=\operatorname{diag}(1,\pm1,\pm1,\dots,\pm1)$ and $|\theta_i|=|\theta_i'|$ for all $i$. Therefore the magnitudes of all Hamiltonian coupling parameters $\{\theta_i\}$ are structurally globally identifiable under the single‑qubit probe measurement of $X_1$ with the probe prepared in an $X_1$ eigenstate.
related.title: Identifiability of exchange model without transverse field (Theorem 1)

variables.title: SPT indicator for existence of economic identification algorithms

variables.content: The nearest-neighbour $2p_{z}$ tight-binding Hamiltonian $H=\sum_{i}\varepsilon_{i}c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{i}-\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\gamma_{0}c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j}$ (with $\varepsilon_{i}=0$ and $\gamma_{0}=3\ \text{eV}$) accurately reproduces the dispersive in-gap bands of the edge-extended graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) of the $N$-AGNR-$S(n,m)$ and $N$-AGNR-$I(n,m)$ families and their SSH-like form. Extracted effective SSH couplings for experimentally relevant examples are: 7-AGNR-S(1,3) $t_{n}=0.45\ \text{eV}$, $t_{m}=0.59\ \text{eV}$; 7-AGNR-I(1,3) $t_{n}=0.45\ \text{eV}$, $t_{m}=0.65\ \text{eV}$. Using these parameters the SSH dispersion $E(k)=\pm\sqrt{t_{n}^{2}+t_{m}^{2}+2t_{n}t_{m}\cos(k)}$ reproduces the tight-binding bands and allows prediction of bandgaps and bandwidths as functions of $(n,m)$, enabling geometric bandgap engineering without changing ribbon width.
variables.title: Quantitative tight-binding parametrization demonstrates SSH-band correspondence and enables bandgap engineering via geometry

variables.content:
For a 100‑site cis‑polyacetylene chain with periodic boundary conditions simulated with a Su–Schrieffer–Heeger (SSH) tight‑binding Hamiltonian modified by a Brazovskii–Kirova symmetry‑breaking term (Brazovskii–Kirova parameter δ0 = 0.05) and the parameter values t0 = 2.5 eV, α = 4.1 eV·Å−1, K = 21 eV·Å−2, and M = 1349.14 eV·fs2·Å−2, a simulated HOMO→LUMO+1 electronic excitation (implemented by changing the single‑particle occupation numbers so that an electron is removed from the highest occupied molecular orbital and placed in the second lowest unoccupied molecular orbital) produces an observable onset of lattice oscillation: the site‑local lattice displacement u_n(t) (with bond variable y_n(t) ≡ u_{n+1}(t) − u_n(t)) yields the bond‑length order parameter
      $$\bar{y}(t)=(-1)^n - \frac{-y_{n-1}(t)+2y_n(t)-y_{n+1}(t)}{4},$$
      and the time series of this order parameter shows the beginning of phonon formation, i.e., the first clear appearance of oscillatory motion of \bar{y}(t), at approximately 200 fs after the HOMO→LUMO+1 excitation.
variables.title: Lattice oscillation onset at ≈200 fs in 100-site SSH cis‑polyacetylene with δ0=0.05

variables.content: For closed quantum systems (unitary evolution, a special case of the GKSL master equation with all decoherence rates zero), the identifiability results for autonomous and controlled open quantum systems reduce to statements about Hamiltonian identifiability. Specifically, an autonomous closed quantum system (governed by the Liouville-von Neumann equation \(\dot{\rho} = -i[H,\rho]\)) maps to an LDS, and its Hamiltonian parameters are identifiable if the input matrix \(\mathbf{B}\) satisfies \(\mathrm{Rank}(\mathbf{B}) = n\) (arbitrary initial state preparation) and the sampling is non-uniform with increments whose ratios are irrational (as in Conclusion 6). A controlled closed quantum system (with Hamiltonian \(H = H_0 + \sum_j u_j(t) H_j\)) maps to a BDS, and its Hamiltonian parameters are identifiable if the bilinear controllability and observability matrices (as in Conclusion 7) have full rank and the system is probed with the family of non-constant pulses \(u_{\tau,\alpha}\) (as in Conclusion 7). In both cases, if the matrix \(\mathbf{M}\) (Conclusion 3) is invertible, the Hamiltonian parameters \(\vec{\theta}\) are uniquely reconstructible from the identified system matrices; since the Kossakowski matrix is zero, the symmetric condition does not apply.

related.content:
Define a bijective vectorization index map \(\Gamma: \{1,2,\dots,n^2\} \to \{(j,k): j,k \in \{1,\dots,n\}\}\) with \(n = N^2-1\). Let \(\mathbf{T}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{n^2 \times n}\) be the matrix whose rows are indexed by \(\Gamma(i)= (j,k)\) and whose entry in column \(l\) is \(-f_{jkl}\), i.e., \((\mathbf{T}_1)_{(j,k), l} = -f_{jkl}\). Let \(\mathbf{T}_2 \in \mathbb{C}^{n^2 \times n^2}\) be the matrix with entries \((\mathbf{T}_2)_{\Gamma(i), \Gamma(j)} = -D^{(i,j)}_{\Gamma(j)}\) where \(D_{lm}^{(a,b)}\) is defined as in Conclusion 1. Assemble the block matrix
      \[
      \mathbf{M} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{T}_1 & \mathbf{T}_2 \\ 0 & \frac{i}{N} \mathbf{T}_1 \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{C}^{(n+n^2) \times (n+n^2)}.
      \]
      If \(\mathbf{M}\) is invertible, then the mapping from the vectorized parameters \((\vec{\theta}, \mathrm{vec}(\gamma))\) to \((\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{A}), \vec{\beta})\) is invertible. Consequently, the Hamiltonian parameters \(\vec{\theta} = (\theta_1,\dots,\theta_n)\) and the entries \(\gamma_{kl}\) of the Kossakowski matrix are uniquely determined by the entries of the system matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) and the vector \(\vec{\beta}\) obtained from the identified LDS or BDS. The relationship is linear via \(\mathbf{M}\), so explicit inversion yields the unique parameter vector.
related.title: Invertibility of M uniquely determines GKSL parameters from the identified LDS/BDS system matrix A and vector β

variables.title: Closed-system identifiability as a special case of open-system results

variables.content:
For the tight‑binding Hamiltonian
      $$
      H=\sum_{j=1}^{L}V\cos(2\pi\beta j+\phi_{1}+\phi_{2})\hat{c}_{j}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{j}
      +[t+i\gamma\sin(2\pi\beta j+\phi_{1})]\hat{c}_{j+1}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{j}
      +[t+i\gamma\sin(2\pi\beta(j+1)+\phi_{1})]\hat{c}_{j}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{j+1},
      $$
      with $V=t=1$, $\gamma=0.05$, $\beta=144/233$, $L=233$, $\phi_{1}=\pi-\pi\beta\pmod{2\pi}$, $\theta=0$ (so $\phi_{2}=-ih$), and $h_{c}=0.68$ for these parameters, eigenstate localization is strongly boundary‑condition sensitive: under open boundary conditions (OBC) the eigenstates are primarily localized even when the periodic boundary condition (PBC) spectrum indicates metallic/extended behavior; under PBC the MI transition is observed with extended states for $h<h_{c}$ and localized states for $h>h_{c}$. Numerical illustrations for $h=0.4$ and $h=1.2$ show representative eigenfunctions localized under OBC for both values, while the same eigenstates are extended under PBC for $h=0.4$ and localized under PBC for $h=1.2$.
variables.title: Boundary‑condition sensitivity: OBC versus PBC eigenstate localization behavior

variables.content:
Define the identifiability observable for any operators $\boldsymbol{O},\boldsymbol{A}$ with $\|\boldsymbol{O}\|,\|\boldsymbol{A}\|\leq 1$, any auxiliary Hamiltonian $\boldsymbol{G}$ and any candidate Hamiltonian $\boldsymbol{K}$ (with interaction degree $d$ and coefficients bounded by $1$) as
$$
Q(\boldsymbol{O},\boldsymbol{G},\boldsymbol{A},\boldsymbol{K}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\mathrm{Tr}[\boldsymbol{O}_{\boldsymbol{G}}^\dagger(t)(h_+(t')\boldsymbol{A}_{\boldsymbol{K}}(t'+t)\rho - h_-(t')\rho\boldsymbol{A}_{\boldsymbol{K}}(t'+t))]g_{\beta}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t'\mathrm{d}t,
$$
where $\rho\propto e^{-\beta\boldsymbol{H}}$ is the unknown Gibbs state of the true Hamiltonian $\boldsymbol{H}$, $\boldsymbol{O}_{\boldsymbol{G}}(t)=e^{i\boldsymbol{G}t}\boldsymbol{O}e^{-i\boldsymbol{G}t}$, $\boldsymbol{A}_{\boldsymbol{K}}(t)=e^{i\boldsymbol{K}t}\boldsymbol{A}e^{-i\boldsymbol{K}t}$, $g_\beta(t)=\frac{2}{\beta}g(2t/\beta)$ with $g(t)=-\frac{\pi^{3/2}}{2\sqrt{2}(1+\cosh(\pi t))}$, and $h_{\pm}(t)$ are rapidly decaying functions defined via the operator Fourier transform with Gaussian window of width $\sigma=1/\beta$ and frequency truncation $\Omega'>0$, satisfying $|h_{\pm}(t)| \lesssim e^{-t^2/\beta^2} \frac{1}{\beta^{3/2}} e^{\beta\Omega'/2 + 1/4}$.
The observable $Q$ has the following properties:
(i) (Vanishing) When $\boldsymbol{K}=\boldsymbol{H}$, $Q(\boldsymbol{O},\boldsymbol{G},\boldsymbol{A},\boldsymbol{H})=0$ for any $\boldsymbol{G},\boldsymbol{O},\boldsymbol{A}$.
(ii) (Robustness/Locality) Let $\boldsymbol{G}_\ell$ and $\boldsymbol{K}_\ell$ be the restrictions of $\boldsymbol{G}$ and $\boldsymbol{K}$ to balls of radius $\ell$ around the supports of $\boldsymbol{O}$ and $\boldsymbol{A}$, respectively. Then
$$
|Q(\boldsymbol{O},\boldsymbol{G},\boldsymbol{A},\boldsymbol{K}) - Q(\boldsymbol{O},\boldsymbol{G}_\ell,\boldsymbol{A},\boldsymbol{K}_\ell)| \lesssim \frac{e^{\beta\Omega'/2}}{\sqrt{\beta}}(e^{-\ell^2/16e^4 d^2\beta^2}+e^{-\pi\ell/e^2 d\beta})(|\boldsymbol{O}|+|\boldsymbol{A}|).
$$
For perturbations that differ only away from the support, similar exponentially decaying bounds hold.
(iii) (Measurability) Each $Q$ can be estimated to additive precision $\epsilon$ with success probability $1-\delta$ using $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{e^{\beta\Omega'}\|\boldsymbol{O}\|^2\|\boldsymbol{A}\|^2}{\beta\epsilon^2}\log(1/\delta)\right)$ copies of $\rho$ and $\operatorname{poly}(\beta, V(\ell), \log(1/(\kappa\epsilon)), \frac{e^{\beta\Omega'/2}}{\sqrt{\beta}})$ quantum gates acting on the neighborhoods of radius $\ell$ around $\boldsymbol{O},\boldsymbol{A}$, where $V(\ell)$ is the number of Hamiltonian terms within distance $\ell$ and $\kappa$ is the precision of the discrete net used for coefficient representation. These properties enable constructing hypothesis tests over local candidate Hamiltonians using only local experiments.
variables.title: Identifiability observable Q and its operational properties

variables.content: A combined, twofold theoretical workflow—parameter-free transfer matrix method (TMM) using measured material optical constants, together with an explicit Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) tight-binding exciton-polariton Hamiltonian—constitutes a practical and general methodology to (i) compute experimentally observable reflectance and field distributions of stacked cavity arrays including realistic loss and vibronic features, and (ii) interpret those observables in terms of microscopic polaritonic bands, Hopfield weights, and topological edge modes. This workflow is applicable beyond the specific organic molecule studied and to inorganic excitons when appropriate material data are supplied.

related.content: For the specific cavity stack with $2N=20$ cavities, $L_c=140$ nm, $L_{\text{odd}}=30$ nm, $L_{\text{even}}=40$ nm, and Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) hopping parameters $v=0.15$, $w=0.09$ for the trivial configuration (and swapped for the topological configuration), the transfer matrix method (TMM) reflectance spectra and the eigenvalues of the SSH tight-binding Hamiltonian show remarkable quantitative agreement: (i) bulk polariton bands, their angle-dependent bandgaps, and the closing of the lower-band gap at large in-plane momentum are reproduced by both methods; (ii) the in-gap edge-state dispersions obtained from the tight-binding diagonalization coincide with reflectance minima and localized field distributions obtained via the TMM, establishing that the multilayer stack physically realizes the SSH exciton-polariton model.
related.title: Quantitative agreement between TMM and SSH tight-binding model for polariton spectra

variables.title: Combined transfer-matrix and SSH tight-binding methodology for topological polariton analysis

variables.content:
The on-site energies $E_q$ and hopping amplitudes $V_{qq'}$ of the effective tight-binding Hamiltonian that maps the electronic Hamiltonian of a Rydberg atom interacting with neutral scatterers can be continuously tuned by varying the arclengths $t_i$ between scatterers along the ring, the ring radius $R$, and the Rydberg principal quantum number $
u$, enabling systematic engineering of nearest-neighbor, staggered, trimerized, and oscillatory long-range couplings in the Rydberg composite. Demonstrations include a system with $
u=60$, $R=2
u^{2}$ for the SSH dimer and trimer SSH examples, and a system with $
u=60$, $R_2=1.74
u^{2}$ for the triangle-chain example (for which the intra-cell coupling $u$ is approximately $-5.5\ \mathrm{MHz}$ for the system with $M=24$ scatterers), showing that geometric parameters map directly onto target tight-binding parameters.
variables.title: Continuous tunability of on-site energies and hopping amplitudes via scatterer geometry and Rydberg quantum number in a Rydberg composite

variables.content: For a zero-temperature, noninteracting (spin-polarized) Fermi gas of N atoms occupying the lowest single-particle eigenstates of the trapped tight-binding Hamiltonian (nearest-neighbour tunnelling amplitude J, harmonic trap spring constant κ), the radial density profile n(r) = ∫_{-∞}^{E_F} ρ(E,r) dE, where ρ(E,r) is the angle-averaged local density of states at radius r (defined as ρ(E,r)=∑_n∫_0^{2π} dφ/(2π) |ψ_n(r)|² δ(E-E_n) with ψ_n and E_n the eigenstates and eigenvalues of the tight-binding Hamiltonian with harmonic confinement), displays a distinct shoulder at the radius where the local Fermi energy E_F - ½κr² crosses the homogeneous-lattice Dirac point energy (E=0). Thus the Dirac-point physics manifests as an observable shoulder at half-filling in the spatial density distribution of the trapped Fermi gas.
variables.title: Signature of Dirac points in the equilibrium density of a trapped noninteracting Fermi gas

variables.content: For the 4-qubit linear chain Hamiltonian $H = \sum_{i=1}^{4}\alpha_i \sigma_i^x + \beta_i \sigma_i^y + \gamma_i \sigma_i^z + \sum_{i=1}^{3}\delta_i \sigma_i^x \sigma_{i+1}^x + \epsilon_i \sigma_i^z \sigma_{i+1}^z$ with all coefficients set to 1, drawing the parameter $\gamma_4$ independently from a Gaussian distribution with mean 0 and variance 1 while leaving the other coefficients at 1 produces, for almost all samples, an observable discrete-time system. Over 30 random realizations of $\gamma_4$, the mean minimal number of discrete steps $k^{*}$ required to reach observability (the smallest $k$ such that the observability matrix attains full rank) was approximately 15.
variables.title: Randomizing a single Hamiltonian parameter generically restores observability; empirics for gamma_4

variables.content: Twelve important hopping interactions between Cu^{2+} ions in three-dimensional Cu_3TeO_6 (cubic, space group Ia\overline{3}, lattice parameter a = 9.537 Å) are identified from a low-energy tight-binding Hamiltonian derived by the Nth-order muffin-tin orbital (NMTO) downfolding method applied to the local-density approximation (LDA) potential, which retains only Cu d_{x^2-y^2} orbitals in the local octahedral frame and integrates out other Cu d orbitals.
variables.title: Twelve hopping interactions between Cu^{2+} ions in Cu_3TeO_6 identified by NMTO downfolding
